2024 Edo Governorship Election Presidential Gubernatorial SYD and the necessity of Kwara’s next promising chapter, By Mustapha Balogun Continuity does not mean standing still; it means taking the gains of the last seven years and scaling them with fresh energy, modern competence, and an unbroken commitment to inclusive development. by Premium Times November 7, 2026 Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Add us on Google As campaigns run from 9 September 2026 to 4 February 2027, voters will ultimately decide, as they should. But looking at the man standing at the door of Ahmadu Bello House, the verdict is clear: SYD’s story is not just about age.
Kwara State stands at a defining crossroads. After more than five decades of existence, the State of Harmony requires a brand of leadership that is neither experimental nor detached from the realities of its people. What Kwara needs at this point is a steady, disciplined, and forward-looking hand, one that understands how systems work, how public resources are managed, and how to translate policy into tangible relief for ordinary citizens.
For too long, Kwara’s past was weighed down by governance that prioritised narrow interests over institutional stability, leaving rural communities disconnected, basic infrastructure neglected, and public trust eroded. Over the last seven years, however, Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq has worked to reset that trajectory: rebuilding institutions, restoring fiscal discipline, and laying down reforms that have given the state a firmer foundation. The future of Kwara depends on protecting and accelerating that momentum. Continuity does not mean standing still; it means taking the gains of the last seven years and scaling them with fresh energy, modern competence, and an unbroken commitment to inclusive development.
This is where a young leader like Salihu Yakubu Danladi, widely known as SYD, steps into the frame. On 27 July 2026, at the Banquet Hall in Ilorin during the APC’s Youth Engagement programme themed “One Kwara Project, One Voice; Youths Driving APC Victory 2027,” Governor AbdulRazaq led young supporters in a thunderous chant: “SYD! SYD!! SYD!!!” A sitting governor does not lend his voice to a chant for just anybody. At 41, SYD represents the bridge between Kwara’s ongoing renewal and its next chapter, a leader who combines the vigour of a new generation with the institutional memory of someone who has helped steer the state’s legislative engine since 2019.
Driving this future requires an arrowhead with a verifiable track record, not empty rhetoric. Born on 31 May 1985 into the royal lineage of Gwanara in Baruten Local Government Area of Kwara North, SYD did not begin his career in the corridors of politics. He started with circuits and systems. He earned his National Diploma and Higher National Diploma in Electrical/Electronic Engineering from Kaduna Polytechnic, followed by a B.Tech from the Federal University of Technology, Minna. After completing his National Youth Service at the National Water Resources Institute in Mando, Kaduna, he worked at FUT Minna from 2010 to 2018 and is a member of both COREN and the Nigerian Society of Engineers. Beyond engineering, he earned an MBA in Revenue Management from Kwara State University, Malete, and a Master’s degree in Peace and Security Studies from Al-Hikmah University, Ilorin, where he is currently pursuing a doctorate. Engineering teaches how systems hold together; revenue management teaches how public money is raised and spent; and peace and security studies teach what happens when communities fall apart.
Since becoming Speaker of the Kwara State House of Assembly in 2019, he has proven that he can manage one of the most demanding offices in any state, balancing competing interests, keeping the House disciplined, and holding the executive to account without undermining the cooperation governance requires. Under his leadership, the Ninth and Tenth Assemblies passed 63 bills and considered more than 100 motions of public importance, while maintaining regular oversight of ministries, departments, and agencies. Landmark legislation, including the Kwara State Public Procurement Law, the Social Investment Programme Law and the Sports Commission Law (both 2019), the Local Government (Miscellaneous Provisions) (Amendment) Law (2019), and the Electric Power Sector Law (2025), alongside the timely passage of annual appropriation acts, provided Governor AbdulRazaq’s reforms with a steady legislative backbone. His influence also extended nationally, serving as Vice Chairman of the APC Northern Speakers’ Forum (2019–2023), Chairman of the APC Conference of Speakers in Nigeria (2024–2026), and a member of the Election Appeal Committee at the 2026 APC National Convention.
Yet, the true test of an arrowhead is what changes in the communities farthest from power. In Baruten and across Kwara North, SYD’s interventions speak for themselves. In water and infrastructure, he helped improve access to clean and safe water, contributed to the realisation of key road projects including the Ilesha-Gwanara Road, and supported the grading of feeder roads to open up rural markets and farms. In security, he facilitated the upgrade of the NSCDC outpost in Gwanara to a Divisional Office and supported the training and equipping of community hunters and vigilantes, many of whom have since been seconded to the National Forest Security Service.
Solar-powered systems, streetlights, grid electricity, renovated primary healthcare centres, and telecommunications facilities have brought previously underserved villages into the fold. In education and empowerment, the establishment of the Federal Science and Technical College in Gwanara, the completion of the KWASU Ilesha-Baruba campus, scholarships, examination sponsorships, agricultural inputs for farmers, and targeted support for artisans, cultural troupes, women’s groups, and youth employment have strengthened livelihoods across the board.

In a crowded field where noise often substitutes for competence, what sets SYD apart is the rare convergence of preparation, performance, and principle. Many aspirants offer ambition without a blueprint, or titles without grassroots impact. SYD brings an engineer’s precision, a legislator’s discipline, a national party figure’s reach, and a grassroots politician’s empathy. Moreover, in over 50 years of Kwara’s existence, no youthful Speaker has ever gone on to succeed a sitting governor. His candidacy also offers Kwara North, a region central to the state’s agricultural economy, geographical spread, and electoral landscape, the opportunity to produce the next governor, a prospect that speaks directly to equity, fairness, and justice in the State of Harmony.
As campaigns run from 9 September 2026 to 4 February 2027, voters will ultimately decide, as they should. But looking at the man standing at the door of Ahmadu Bello House, the verdict is clear: SYD’s story is not just about age. It is about capacity, proven competence, and the readiness to lead Kwara into its most promising chapter yet.
